## Jacobian Matrix

In [[vector-calculus]] the **Jacobian matrix** of a vector function
$\boldsymbol{f}:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ collects all of its first-order
partial derivatives. It is the natural generalisation of the derivative to
vector-valued functions. If the matrix is square ($n=m$) its determinant is
the **Jacobian determinant**.

:::{.definition data-title="Jacobian Matrix"}

Let $\boldsymbol{f}:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ be a vector function whose
first-order partial derivatives all exist. The **Jacobian matrix**
$J_{\boldsymbol{f}}$ is the $m\times n$ matrix with $(i,j)$-th entry
$\frac{\partial f_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}$:

$$
J_{\boldsymbol{f}}=\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_{1}} & \cdots &
\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_{n}}
\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}
\nabla^{\top}f_{1} \\
\vdots \\
\nabla^{\top}f_{m}
\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}
\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x_{1}} & \cdots &
\frac{\partial f_{1}}{\partial x_{n}} \\
\vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\
\frac{\partial f_{m}}{\partial x_{1}} & \cdots &
\frac{\partial f_{m}}{\partial x_{n}}
\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $\nabla^{\top}f_{i}$ is the row vector given by the transpose of the
[[gradient]] of the $i$-th component (see [[vector-calculus-identities]]).

:::

:::{.example}

Let $f(x,y)=(2x^2+3xy,\ 4y^2x+2x)$. Then
$$
J_{f}=\begin{bmatrix}
4x+3y & 3x \\
4y^2+2 & 8xy
\end{bmatrix},
$$
and the Jacobian determinant is
$$
\det(J_{f})=8xy(4x+3y)-3x(4y^2+2)=32x^2y+12xy^2-6x.
$$
The Jacobian describes the change in the *new* coordinates with respect to
the *old* coordinates.

:::

### Best Linear Approximation

If $\boldsymbol{f}$ is differentiable at $\boldsymbol{x}^*\in\mathbb{R}^n$ then
its differential is represented by $J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\boldsymbol{x}^*)$, and
the linear map $\boldsymbol{h}\mapsto J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\boldsymbol{x}^*)
\boldsymbol{h}$ is the **best linear approximation** of $\boldsymbol{f}$ near
$\boldsymbol{x}^*$:

$$
\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})-\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}^*)=
J_{\boldsymbol{f}}(\boldsymbol{x}^*)(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}^*)
+o(\lVert\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}^*\rVert),\qquad
\boldsymbol{x}\to\boldsymbol{x}^*,
$$

where $o(\lVert\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}^*\rVert)$ is a remainder that
vanishes faster than $\lVert\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}^*\rVert$. For $n=m=1$
this is the degree-one [[taylor-series]] approximation
$f(x)-f(x^*)=f'(x^*)(x-x^*)+o(x-x^*)$, so the Jacobian is the first-order
derivative of a vector function.

### Chain Rule

:::{.theorem data-title="Jacobian Chain Rule"}

For composable differentiable functions $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$ and
$g:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}^k$, and $x\in\mathbb{R}^n$,
$$
J_{g\circ f}(x)=J_{g}(f(x))\,J_{f}(x).
$$

:::

:::{.proof}

By the best linear approximation of $f$ at $x$ and of $g$ at $f(x)$, with
$h\to0$,
$$
g(f(x+h))=g\bigl(f(x)+J_{f}(x)h+o(\lVert h\rVert)\bigr)
=g(f(x))+J_{g}(f(x))J_{f}(x)h+o(\lVert h\rVert).
$$
The matrix multiplying $h$ is the Jacobian of $g\circ f$ at $x$. This is the
matrix form of the [[chain-rule]].

:::

### Inverse

By the inverse function theorem, if $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ has a
continuous Jacobian that is non-singular at $x$, then $f$ is invertible on a
neighbourhood of $x$, i.e. it is **locally invertible**. The Jacobian of the
inverse is the matrix inverse of the Jacobian,
$$
J_{f^{-1}}(y)=J_{f}(f^{-1}(y))^{-1},\qquad
\det J_{f^{-1}}(y)=\frac{1}{\det J_{f}(f^{-1}(y))}.
$$
This follows from the chain rule applied to $f\circ f^{-1}=\mathrm{id}$. These
formulas drive the [[change-of-variables-formula]].

### Critical Points

For a differentiable $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^m$, a **critical point** is
a point where the rank of $J_{f}$ is not maximal, i.e. is smaller than
$\min(n,m)$. For $m=1$ these are the points where $\nabla f=0$; for $n=m$ they
are the points where $\det J_{f}=0$.

## Hessian Matrix

The **Hessian matrix** is the second-order analogue of the Jacobian, for a
scalar field. It describes the **local curvature** of a multivariate
function. It is usually denoted $H$ (historically also $\nabla\nabla$,
$\nabla^2$, $\nabla\otimes\nabla$ or $D^2$).

:::{.definition data-title="Hessian Matrix"}

Let $f:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ have all second-order partial derivatives.
The **Hessian matrix** of $f$ is the $n\times n$ matrix
$$
(H_{f})_{i,j}:=\frac{\partial^2 f}{\partial x_{i}\partial x_{j}}.
$$
Its determinant is the **Hessian determinant**.

:::

If the second partial derivatives are continuous, then $H_{f}$ is a
**symmetric matrix** by the symmetry of mixed partial derivatives. The Hessian
is the Jacobian of the gradient, transposed:
$$
H_{f}(x)=J_{\nabla f}(x)^{\top}.
$$
(The two coincide when $H_f$ is symmetric.)

:::{.example}

For $f(x,y)=x^2y+y^3$,
$$
\nabla f=\begin{pmatrix}2xy\\ x^2+3y^2\end{pmatrix},\qquad
H_{f}=\begin{bmatrix}2y & 2x\\ 2x & 6y\end{bmatrix},
$$
which is symmetric, as expected.

:::

### Applications to Optimisation

The Hessian is the coefficient of the quadratic term in the second-order
[[taylor-series|Taylor expansion]]
$$
f(\boldsymbol{x}+\Delta\boldsymbol{x})\approx f(\boldsymbol{x})
+\nabla f(\boldsymbol{x})^{\top}\Delta\boldsymbol{x}
+\tfrac{1}{2}\Delta\boldsymbol{x}^{\top}H_{f}(\boldsymbol{x})\Delta\boldsymbol{x}.
$$
At a critical point ($\nabla f=0$) the sign of the quadratic form decides the
type of the point: a minimum if $H_f$ is positive definite, a maximum if it is
negative definite and a saddle if it is indefinite (see
[[matrices#Quadratic Forms and Positive Definiteness|positive definite
matrices]]). Newton-type methods in [[optimization]] use this expansion to
choose their steps.

Computing and storing the full Hessian takes $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ memory, which
is infeasible for high-dimensional problems such as the loss functions of
neural networks or statistical models with many parameters.
